been that it has been hooked up too much to political pull and patronage and not sufficiently hooked up to ordinary businesslike and efficient methods. That is the difficulty with the Intercolonial Railway, but I shall come to that later on. The minister desires that it shall be hooked up to some great Canadian railway system. Let us go back for a moment to ten and eleven years ago, let us go back to the proposals of the government in 1897 and 1898. I very well remember the discussion of those years because I was a new member in this House, and was naturally attracted by a very important debate such as that, especially as it had reference to the Intercolonial Railway in which the members from the maritime provinces feel an absorbing interest. What was the proposal of the government at that time? It had entered into a contract with the Drummond County Railway and another with the Grand Trunk Railway, and I would point out to the Minister of Railways the glowing predictions uttered at that time. A very able gentleman then occupied the position of Minister of Railways and Canals, the late Hon. Mr. Blair. At page 4264 of the ' Hansard ' of that year Mr. Blair, speaking for the government, to the parliament of Canada and to the people of Canada, said:
The idea has gone abroad and has sunk deeply in people's minds, that because the Intercolonial Railway has not been a paying property-or, in other words, has scarcely in all its history been able to show a balance on the right side of its accounts-there was something inherently vicious in the government ownership of railways, and that the less a government had to do with them the better. That was an idea which I think I am justified in saying strongly impressed itself upon the people's minds. But I think I shall be able to show this committee that if there has been one thing more than another which has led to this state of affairs, it is that the Intercolonial Railway has been cribbed, cabined and confined. I will give this committee, before I get through, good reasons for believing that after this extension shall be concluded, and after it shall have an opportunity of getting into successful competition, the days of deficits will be over, and we shall be able-I do not say to pay interest on the capital invested- I do not think the country looks for that- but by the business arrangements which we shall be in a position to make, and by the facilities which will be secured to us in Montreal, to show a balance on the right side of the account and to reverse the record which has been exhibited in the running operations of this railway in times past.
Further on:
I do say, as far as I have been able to exercise any little judgment I may have, that the extension of this railway to the city of Montreal will reverse the position it has had in the past by creating business which cannot fail to produce vastly important results.
Then at page 4269:
But the fact, as I say, that we have carried only a small proportion of through passengers and through freight in times past, shows under what disadvantages the road has been operated. We look for an entire change in this respect.
Further on:
And, as I was saying a moment ago, if you examine the details of the contract which has been entered into between the government on one hand and these companies on the other, you will perceive very clearly that we have been solicitous and careful, that every term and every condition should be introduced which would ensure us an opportunity to gain our share of the western trade. As you will see, we have engaged with the Grand Trunk to carry the freights for us from the west to Montreal and to deliver these freights to us when they get them there, not to take them around by the Richmond line or by Levis-not to carry them off on the Grand Trunk, but to deliver them to us. So, when we send our canvassing agents through the west, as all railway companies do, and ought to do, and those agents pick up traffic and make contracts, we may be sure that the business will fall into our hands when it reaches Montreal.
From this you will observe the position taken by the government at that time. Mr. Sifton expressed it during the debate of 1903 in a still more striking way. He said that the Intercolonial Railway had had its terminus in a ploughed field and they had brought that terminus to the city of Montreal and had placed that railroad in a position to compete for and obtain its fair share of the great traffic of the west. The government in 1903 had made a contract with the Grand Trunk, the terms of which are embodied in ' Hansard ' at page 4088 et seq. The government claimed that this contract with the Grand Trunk Railway would enable the government of this country, by the agreement thus constituted, to obtain its fair share of western traffic and through traffic and that it would necessarily result in placing the Intercolonial Railway on an entirely different basis from that which it had occupied in days gone by. There were to be no more deficits, the Intercolonial Railway was to obtain its fair share of western traffic and the agreement thus consummated by the government was to result in an absolute revolution in the returns which the people of this country were to expect from the Intercolonial Railway. We have had 10 years' experience with that contract. What is the answer of the Minister of Railways to-day? His answer to the people of this country, his answer to the parliament of this country, is practically that the agreement of 1897 and 1898 between the government of Canada and the Grand Trunk has resulted absolutely in no change or benefit to the Intercolonial Railway or the people of Canada, that the agreement has been practically evaded, that it has not resulted

in the Intercolonial Railway obtaining any fair or proportionate share of western traffic. I ask hon. gentlemen of this House and the people of this country, in the light of that, how much we are to expect from the agreements which this government in
1903	and again in 1904 made with the Grand Trunk Pacific Company, which is only another name, after all, for the Grand Trunk Railway?
Mr. Speaker, it seems to me that the Minister of Railways and Canals in the address which he delivered this afternoon, has unwittingly passed about as severe a criticism upon the agreements of 1903 and
1904	as have ever been addressed to the parliament or the people of this country. He has shown the absolute futility of any such agreement whether contained in the Act of 1897 or the Act of 1903, so far as the purpose may have been to divert traffic over the Grand Trunk Railway from Portland in the United States, to the Canadian ports in the maritime provinces. Under these circumstances, how does my hon. friend propose to get the Intercolonial Railway hooked up to any great railway system in Canada to a greater extent than it was hooked up to the Grand Trunk Railway by the agreement of 1897. How is it possible to devise an agreement which, on the face of it, would be stronger or apparently more effective for that purpose ? My hon. friend would not, I think, be prepared to suggest how that agreement, in its terms, could be made stronger. Yet we see the result. Every prediction of the government in 1897 has been falsified, not only in the spirit but the letter. The deficits, instead of disappearing, have increased, and we are faced to-day with a deficit of half a million dollars. The only reply which the minister can give is one that cannot very well be confirmed, and that is the people of the maritime provinces are getting lower freight rates than the people of any other province.

I was speaking about the lower rates without any particular reference to this year. The deficit this year is largely attributable to the vast falling off in traffic which has taken place on all railways. The falling off up to December 31, was over half a million dollars.

I do not desire that my remarks as to the results of the operations of the Intercolonial Railway shall be confined by any means to the year we are now considering, because it is well known that when every other railway worthy of the name on this continent was earning dividends on the capital invested in it, the Intercolonial Railway was considered to have made an excellent showing if it came out without a deficit or with a surplus of a few thousand dollars. There must be some explanation of this. The opposition took Mr. R. L. BORDEN.
a certain position in this regard in 1903, when the government brought down its proposal. I am not going to argue the case over again but will simply invite attention to what we then proposed. I moved a resolution in that session declaring, among other things, the following :
That this House is of the opinion that the Intercolonial Railway and the Prince Edward Island Railway should continue to be owned and operated by the government of Canada.
That the government system of railways should be developed and improved in the province of Quebec and the maritime provinces, and should also be extended from Montreal westward to such point or points as will enable it to transport to eastern Canada and to our national ports on the St. Lawrence and on the Atlantic the rapidly increasing products of our great western country.
That the management of government railways and of all railways, under the control or direction of the government, should be tree from party political control, influence and interference.
In the same session, or the session following, there were questions put and answers brought down which indicated that the Intercolonial Railway, if it had been operated froip Parry Sound to Halifax, could have carried grain at a rate which would have shown a profit and which would also have ensured to it a fair share of the western traffic. However, I shall not go over that portion of my argument more than to recall to hon. members the fact that we did take that position at that time.
My hon. friend the Minister of Railways has spoken of bettering the condition by leasing the Intercolonial Railway to some great railway corporation. If that policy, he said, is not adopted and carried out, then it will be necessary for the government to adopt the suggestion of the hon. member for Westmoreland (Mr. Emmerson) and acquire certain branch lines in the maritime provinces, especially the province of New Brunswick. I fail to understand how the acquisition of these branch lines in New Brunswick will bring us to our share of that western traffic which, according to every minister of railways, whom I have heard discuss the subject, is absolutely necessary to the future success and operation of the government road. The acquisition of branch lines in New Brunswick will not give us any special advantage in securing our fair share of the great western traffic to which we are looking in the future. Nor do I see how the acquisition of these branch lines is going to offset the disadvantage relied upon by the Minister of Railways-if it be a disadvantage-of the low rates which he says the people of the maritime provinces enjoy at present as compared with the people of the rest of Canada. Yet my hon. friend puts the two as alternatives. He

says there are only two things to do. One is to lease the Intercolonial Railway to some great railway corporation; the other is to acquire these branch lines. Take the latter alternative, will any man tell me how the acquisition of these branch lines in the province of New Brunswick will remedy the disadvantages of which the minister has spoken? I may be singularly obtuse, but I cannot understand how that will get the Intercolonial Railway out of the difficulties into which, according to the minister, it is now plunged.
I do not know whether or not the Minister of Railways is considering the other alternative. The question was put across the floor in the early part of the session, and the answer of the government was that there had been certain proposals made to it in that regard, but that these proposals were not even considered. But now we come to another important, and a very important part, of the minister's argument this afternoon. He said that some change might be necessary. I think he went so far as to say that in his opinion some change was necessary in the management of the Intercolonial Railway, and he spoke of the appointment of a board. My hon. friend from South Lanark (Mr. Haggart) has referred to my proposal of some years ago that the Intercolonial Railway ought to be placed under the management of a committee. Mr. Speaker, I have not the slightest confidence in, nor do I place the slightest reliance on the word 'board' or the word 'commission,' but I do place some reliance on the management of the Intercolonial Railway by business methods and the absolute elimination of party political control. I do not say, mark you, the elimination of political control or interference. By political interference I mean political in the highest sense of the word. It may be absolutely right and proper that the government and parliament should on occasion exercise what you might call political control in connection with the management of the Intercolonial Railway. But what I am referring to is party political interference, that political patronage, that party pull, which tends to make the Intercolonial Railway, whether the one party or the other be in power, a great political machine. I know, from my own experience in the maritime provinces, that there are certain party hacks there who regard the Intercolonial Railway as belonging to the Liberal party, while that party is in power, and not as belonging to the people of Canada, but to be used for the ends of the party so long as it remains in office. And I am not party man enough to deny that if the Conservatives were in power, there might be men calling themselves Conservatives who would have as fantastic and as absurd a view regarding the ownership and management of that road.
The essential thing that requires to be done is to put the management of the Intercolonial Railway under such conditions that the party hack should have no right to interfere. My hon. friend says that the management of the Intercolonial Railway is to-day all that it should be. I know something about the management of the Intercolonial Railway, and I do not believe that it is to-day what it should be. I believe that there are men by the score, by the hundred, on the Intercolonial who are not bound by the ordinary ties of discipline, because forsooth they were put where they are by political pull and interference; and that same political pull and interference prevents them from submitting to that discipline which is absolutely essential to the proper arid efficient management of any railway. I know whereof I am speaking, and if it were necessary or desirable I could give some illustrations of that fact. The name amounts to nothing; the principle amounts to a great deal; and when my hon. friend the Minister of Railways and Canals tells us that government responsibility would be to some extent interfered with, I venture to think that he speaks, if I may say so without offence, a little without the book. What have we been doing in Canada in recent years? Did we not appoint a commission to superintend and carry on the construction of the Transcontinental Railway? I suppose that was an endeavour to take that work out of party politics, if it were possible to do so by appointing men to carry it on separately from any department of the government. Have we not appointed a Civil Service Commission, and is not government responsibility, in the sense in which my hon. friend spoke, interfered with somewhat by the appointment of that commission? And did we not three or four years ago appoint a Railway Commission for Canada, which has to-day imposed upon it some of the duties, and which under the statutes of this country has assumed some of the functions which were formerly discharged by the Railway Committee of the Privy Council, consisting of members of the government?
I venture to think-and I am speaking to business men who will I am sure weigh my words-that when the government of any country undertakes to engage in a business such as that of transportation, some of the old ideas about govermental responsibility will have to be modified a little. The business of transportation in Great Britain, in the United States, and m this country has been committed almost entirely to private enterprise. As my hon. friend from South Lanark (Mr. Haggart)

has well remarked, it is not so in other countries; because if you eliminate Great Britain and the United States, you will find that at least1 two-thirds of the railways of the world are owned and for the most part operated by the state. But in Great Britain and the United States, it is not so. Therefore when we in Canada engage in a business which in the great English speaking countries of the world has been committed to private enterprise-when we engage in that business in competition with private enterprise, it seems to me that we ought not to be bound too much by the fetters of that governmental responsibility to which my hon. friend the Minister of Railways and Canals attaches so much importance. Suppose the parliament of Canada put the Intercolonial Railway under a commission or a board, or under the management of one man-these are details as to which I care nothing-and give to that man a status which would enable him to manage the road free from party patronage, free from political pull, free from political interference, the parliament of Canada could take back what it had given, and, if it found that that system was not a successful system, it could revert to the earlier methods or seek some new method of dealing with the railway. You do not take away any of the responsibility of parliament or of the government except for the time being, and you take it away only in respect of the operation of the road and in order that it may be carried on as an efficient business enterprise and by efficient business methods. Therefore, I venture to think that the suggestion which has been made in this regard ought not to be put aside too lightly by the Minister of Railways and Canals. He speaks of a board of four men, but he is absolutely nebulous as to what their duties and responsibilities shall be. You have a general manager of the Intercolonial Railway now. What would it advantage the Intercolonial Railway or the people of this country if you appoint four men and leave the methods of operation exactly as they are at present? You might as well appoint Ministers of Railways and Canals and expect good results as to do that. What we must arrive at by any satisfactory solution of this question, which has been under discussion for the past twenty-five years, is some means of applying to the management of the Intercolonial Railway just ordinary, plain, honest business methods. Three or four years ago we advocated making the Intercolonial Railway subject to the Railway Commission just like any ordinary railway in this country. I see no reason why that should not be done. Whether the Minister of Railways and Canals appoints a board, a commission or one man, I think that he will arrive at good results, he will accomplish more than any of his prede-Mr. R. L. BORDEN.
cessors have accomplished, if he will so frame his statute and his regulations that the road will be carried on by the same methods that private enterprise has applied to the transportation business. If he does that, I venture to think that good results will follow.
I see no reason why the Intercolonial Railway should not be operated successfully There seems to be an impression in the minds of some of the hon. members of this House that the Intercolonial Railway runs through a wilderness. Why, it runs through some of the finest districts in Canada, in the province of Nova Scotia, the province of New Brunswick and the province of Quebec. Is the country between Quebec and Montreal not one of the finest districts in Canada? Does not the Intercolonial Railway in the province of New Brunswick run through a splendid fertile region, with great timber and other resources of many kinds? Does not the Intercolonial in the province of Nova Scotia run through a thickly populated country, and is it not carrying the freight of great enterprises such as the Dominion Iron & Steel corporation and the Nova Scotia Steel Company? And can you imagine a finer district anywhere in the Dominion than that portion of the province of Nova Scotia through which it runs? I do not put out of sight the consideration that the minister has placed before the House in respect of the competition of water carriers; but let no one imagine that the Intercolonial is running through a wilderness. It is running through just as good a country as there is on the face of the earth to-day, and there is no reason why it should not be carried on by honest, straight business methods; and there is no reason that I can understand why it should not be operated successfully and bring a fair return, or some return at least on the very large amount of capital which the people of this country have put into it.
With regard to the question of branch lines, that has been very fully debated, and I do not intend to touch upon it to-night. I would be in sympathy with any reasonable movement for providing feeders for the Intercolonial Railway in the maritime provinces or the province of Quebec. My view of the Intercolonial is that it cannot stand still; it must develop or we must give it up, one or the other. You will not find any live Tailway in Canada today that is in a condition of stagnation. The people of Canada and the government of Canada must both make up their minds to either one thing or the other, to give up the Intercolonial altogether, as my hon. friend the Minister of Railways partly suggested this afternoon, that is, pass it over to some private corporation, or to develop that railway, to apply the same enterprise

and efficient business methods, not only to the operation of the road, but to its development, which we might expect if the road was absolutely transferred in title to a corporation. There can be no half way measure about it, it must either be efficiently developed or it must be handed over to some corporation. I rose, however, in the main, for the purpose of pointing out to the Minister of Railways that the glowing predictions of his predecessor of the results of the extension to Montreal, have not been fulfilled, and to point out the extreme difficulty of accomplishing such results as were predicted in that case, by the mere terms of a contract. That has not been possible in the case of the extension of the Intercolonial to Montreal, and it will not be possible, I think, under the contract which this government, in 1903-4, entered into with the Grand Trunk Pacific.

I am sure that any one who has been at all familiar with the part which I have taken in discussions with respect to the Intercolonial, will not condemn me for prolonging somewhat this debate. My voice has been heard at this session already, and on former occasions I have felt impelled to give an expression of my views. I have listened with the closest attention to that which has fallen from the lips of the hon. gentlemen who have preceded me this afternoon and evening, and I am bound to say that I have not been able to elicit very much comfort from anything that has been said either on one side or the other. You, Sir, will agree with me that it is a lonesome task to plough a lone furrow; and when I listened to the remarks of the Minister of Railways and to the subsequent remarks of the hon. member for South Lanark (Mr. Haggart) with respect to the Intercolonial and its branch lines, and when I listened with close attention to the remarks of the leader of the opposition, it will be understood that I could not get much comfort from any of them. It is a somewhat unpleasant position to stand half way between, and to find none who agree with the views which I hold with respect to so great a question as the Intercolonial Railway. Let my attitude not be mistaken. I have now been in public life upwards of twenty-five years, and I have never yet, and never will be, charged with being an opportunist, or with concealing my convictions on public questions, whether they are adverse to one party or the other. It may be said that I hold extreme views with respect to the Intercolonial; that may be true, but they are honestly held, and are the Tesult of a life studv of the conditions which prevail on that Toad, are the result of a familiarity with it that could only be obtained by the association which I have been permitted
to have with the employees who are engaged on that road, and by the knowledge I have of the people of the maritime provinces and of the conditions which that railway is designed to meet.	_
Now, Sir, I can congratulate the Minister of Railways and Canals on the very able speech which he made this afternoon. I think that if ever there was a speech delivered that was confirmatory of the attitude I have taken in this House, it was the speech of my hon. friend the Minister of Railways. It will be borne in mind perhaps that the views which I hold are, in the first place, that we should continue to own and operate the Intercolonial as a government road, and that its operation should be expanded, that it should be developed in every Tespect. I am sure that in the very clear, and concise, and eloquent speech delivered by the Minister of Railways, every point that I have taken with respect to that railway has been established, has been demonstrated beyond question.
Why was not the minister's speech a comfort to the hon. gentleman ?

My hon. friend need not anticipate. He has established my premises, he has supported every assertion I have ever made, he has demonstrated by comparison with other railways that the Intercolonial has been one of the best managed railways in Canada, that it has been efficiently managed, that its rates are low, that its earnings are as a consequence small, that its expenses are not great in comparison with those of other railways; he has demonstrated all these, and he has shown that the Intercolonial has served a great purpose. He started out with saying that, as a first condition, we must remember that the Intercolonial was a set-off of the canals, that they were both to be viewed in the same light at the time of confederation, that they were designed to come down through the decades of our life as a confederation in that same relative position, the one off-setting the other.
My hon. friend the Minister of Railways and Canals clearly agreed with that condition. Then he brings out the point that it is the duty of this parliament, as it is the duty of the people of the country, to recognize the Intercolonial and the_ canals as twin systems, each to be treated in precisely and practically the same way, the one serving as a highway for central Canada and the other as a highway for eastern Canada as well as for central Canada with Tespect to its traffic. He proved that beyond all question, and my hon. friend the leader of the opposition only took exception^ to one point in the argument of my hon. friend the Minister of Railways and Canals. He joined issue upon the question as to the tariff

rates of the Intercolonial Railway, My hon. friend the leader of the opposition states that he wants it demonstrated to him that the rates prevailing on the Intercolonial are lower. I did, on a former occasion, I think, two years ago, place on the table of this House the tariff rates prevailing on the Grand Trunk, the tariff rates prevailing on the Canadian Pacific Railway, the passenger rates and traffic rates prevailing on these respective railways, and I, at the same moment, placed before this House the passenger and freight rates' prevailing on the Intercolonial. I need only remind the House of that which demonstrated clearly and beyond question on that occasion, that the freight rates on the Intercolonial Railway with respect to every classification of freight were lower than on either of the other railways. I showed then what increase per cent of the Grand Trunk and Canadian Pacific rates over the Intercolonial rates was. on certain classes of freight. I gave the rate with respect to different distances, commencing with five and over ten miles and ranging up to 700 miles, I pointed out the difference both as to export tariff rates and as to the ordinary tariff rates and I also pointed out that the increases over the Intercolonial rates ranged all the way from fifty to one hundred per cent with respect to certain classifications." I called the attention of parliament at that time to the local comparative rates on coal in carloads, and I showed then, in comparison with other railways, that the Intercolonial rates were from 25 to 10 per cent lower dependent upon distance. I also showed that with respect to lumber, to give one illustration, the rates on a 650 to 700 mile haul on the Intercolonial are 57 per cent lower than the export rates on either of the other railways, and with respect to the ordinary haul 76 per cent lower than they are on either the Canadian Pacific Railway or Grand Trunk Railway. The passenger rates were found to be lower dependent upon the mileage. Hon. members need only turn to the ' Hansard ' of 1907, page 5338 and following pages, to find confirmation of the statements whicli I am now making. If my hon. friend the leader of the opposition is anxious to know he can there learn because these are the actual freight tariff rates prevailing on these railways. The originals, as they came from the railways, were presented to parliament and the facts and statements were there made. Only in that respect was there any difference between my hon. friend the leader of the opposition and my hon. friend the Minister of Railways and Canals with respect to the Itercolonial Railway. I have said that I do not get very much comfort even if my position with respect to the Intercolonial Railway as to its operation has been established by the remarks oj my hon. friend the Minister of Railways and Mr. EMMERSON.
Canals because of his conclusions. He has, after saying that the railway had been efficiently managed, that there was nothing wrong with it, that its administration could not be better in comparison with that of other railways, asked the question: What shall we do with the road? Why is it necessary to do anything with the road? He has clearly shown that during the past year, in common with the other railways on this continent, that railway had a decrease in its earning power that has been very marked particularly in the maritime provinces because of the depression in the lumber traffic. It will be borne in mind that the lumber traffic of the Intercolonial represents 26 per cent of its whole traffic, and I am sure that T am within the facts when I state that there has been a practical stagnation in the matter of the transportation of lumber along the Intercolonial during the past twelve months in consequence of the condition of the lumber trade in Great Britain. In that particular alone there has been an immense falling off in the earnings of the Intercolonial Railway and the falling off in that regard has been followed by a lessening of its earning power in other respects, to the extent, as the Minister of Railways and Canals has shown, of $500,000. He has shown that, despite that falling off and despite an increase in the wages paid to the employees, there is only an anticipated deficit of half a million dollars this year. Have we not had a surplus on the Intercolonial Railway for the past five years? Then, what is there to complain of? What is there to be done? If the management of the Intercolonial has been good, in comparison with that of other railways in Canada, if there is nothing to complain of with respect to it in that regard, why should it be condemned simply because there have been deficits? Surely, Mr. Speaker, that will not be contended in this House. We had a report laid on the table of the House the other day showing that the deficit of the Welland canal alone, during the past five years had averaged nearly $180,000 per year. Some hon. member lias computed the figures with respect to the deficits on the Intercolonial from 1867 down to the present and has shown that the average deficits on the Intercolonial, commencing with its inception, when it was a railway running from Riviere du Loup to Halifax, Moncton and St. John, have only been about $245,000. On that one little canal alone there is an annual loss of $170,000. Is there talk of doing anything about that? The minister has told us that the canals of Canada are a balance of the Intercolonial Railway, but if you add but one other canal you will have a greater annual deficit on these two canals than you have all told on the Intercolonial Railway. Of course, if you take the canals of Canada as a whole

there will be, according to the statement oi the minister himself, a deficit of upwards of one and a quarter million dollars. How is it we never hear the question asked. What shall we do with the canals, or, shall we put them under a commission, or, shall we transfer them to a private corporation in the interests of the country? If these questions are asked about the Intercolonial, surely they could with equal reason be asked about the canals which also have deficits.
Of course the hon. gentleman is aware that the traffic on the canals is free to the whole country. There is no analogy between them and the Intercolonial Railway.

I am thankful to my hon. friend for the information, but I think there is a great analogy for there is an investment of $90,000,000 of the people's money in the canals and an investment of $80,000,000 of the peoples' money in the Intercolonial both investments being to develop the trade of the country. But there is this additional point in favour of the Intercolonial, that its construction was undertaken as well to bring about the confederation of the then scattered provinces into one Dominion.
My disappointment at the speech of the Minister of Railways is to be found in the fact that his conclusions do not seem to agree with his argument. He argued that the excellent management of the Intercolonial under government operation showed up well in comparison with the private operation of privately owned railways, and that while the results of the book-keeping were not so favourable to the Intercolonial yet that was brought about by peculiar conditions. I agree with the Minister of Railways up to that point. However, he concludes that although the government administration of the railway is good and although the Minister of Railways through his department can manage it in excellent fashion, and although the conditions justify low rates, yet he says we must go back to company operation before the Intercolonial Railway can be made a success. A success in what way? The hon. gentleman proposes to make it a success by trying an experiment. He proposes to form a board of management, a sort of advisory board he says. But let me ask: What is the necessity for an advisory board or a managing board if the management is as excellent as he said it was under the present administration.	*
Hear, hear.

Why the necessity for any change? If the minister brushes aside the question of placing this railway under an independent commissioner or commissioners, independent of this government or
of any future government and only answerable to parliament; if he declines to place that railway under the direction of a servant of this parliament, then, what is the necessity for turning aside' from the excellent management of the railway during the past few years,-and I agree with him that the management has been excellent. If it is desirable to have a board of management then I would invite the attention of the minister to the character of the board.
I understand from him that three of the gentlemen who are to comprise that board are now connected with the Department of Railways. One of them is the deputy minister, and a very able deputy minister he is as I have had opportunity of knowing. The other two are to be men who have been for years in the employ of the Intercolonial and who have had the management and control of it under the Department of Railways. If this is to be an advisory board we have had for many years the advantage of the advice of these two gentlemen, and we have had for four or five years past the advantage of the great experience and knowledge of the deputy Minister of Railways. I do not know to whom the minister refers when he speaks of two other gentlemen who have been for years in the employment of the Intercolonial Railway, but I suppose I can assume that they are gentlemen who have controlled and managed the Intercolonial Railway in the past. Is that management going to be any better because they are clustered together in a board? Assuming that one of them is the present manager of the Intercolonial Railway, are you going to have him any more efficient or any more alive by attaching him to others and making it a hydraheaded management ? I do not think so. I ask the minister, and I ask hon. gentlemen to consider how it can be expected that any better results will be obtained in the management of the road from these very same men. Well, sir, I do not look for any great success, nor do I look for any great improvement in that direction.
I should be glad indeed to see the hopes of the minister realized but I cannot now see anything but failure written all around the proposition and in that I think many hon. members who have a knowledge of the conditions will agree with me. But that is neither -here nor there, I simply call the minister's attention to it. I asked myself what my hon. friend meant when he said that if this experiment failed these other questions would be considered. What other questions ? Is it the transference of the Intercolonial Railway to a company-operated road? I would hope that that question had been settled in the mind of the minister. He has convinced me and I believe, he has convinced the country that he can manage the Intercolonial Railway efiiciently. He has

demonstrated to this House this afternoon that it is possible to so manage the Intercolonial that it will be in the interests of the people and that it will become what it was designed to be a government-operated road in the interests of the country. The very moment you discuss the question whether the government of this country shall part with the Intercolonial Railway, you are face to face with one great issue, whether you will have a government-operated railway or whether the people will tolerate a railway-operated government, surely the time has not come when we cannot operate that railway, when we cannot as a people manage the railway in the interests of the people. If it should be shown to me that the Intercolonial Railway could be managed under some system with greater advantage to the people of Canada, that it would develop the east to a greater extent under a private corporation, I would be willing to accept that alternative, but the prevailing opinion to-day is in favour of that measure of government-operation which we have. That feeling is not confined to eastern Canada, you will find it in Ontario and in the west. That opinion should be recognized by this parliament.
I quite admit that the corporations are anxious to secure the road. The minister has pointed out that the Canadian Pacific Railway already have access to the Atlantic coast and that in a very few years the Grand Trunk Pacific will find an outlet there. He says then that there must be an outlet for another railway and that the Intercolonial Railway offers an excellent outlet for some trans-continental line of railway. There are only three railroads that have aspirations towards becoming transcontinental ; the Canadian Pacific Railway is now a transcontinental line, the Grand Trunk Pacific is seeking to become one and we intend that it shall be, the Canadian Northern hope to become one. The possession of the Intercolonial Railway by the Canadian Northern Railway would be of immense advantage to the Canadian Northern. Their system is now oO miles west of Edmonton and they hope to reach the Pacific coast. They connect Edmonton and Port Arthur. I read in the newspaper press that there are now proposals to supply the link between Port Arthur and Sudbury. Soon they will have a through line from Sudbury to _ Montreal. There will still be a missing link between Montreal and the sea-board and it would be of immense advantage to them to reach Halifax or Cape Breton. They would then be in contact with their Nova Scotia system. They have a line of railway from Halifax westward around the south coast of Nova Scotia, known as the Halifax and South Western.
If they could connect their western system with their eastern system it would be a great advantage to them, and I do not say Mr. EMMERSON.
they are not justified in having hopes and aspirations in that direction. The question is, is it in the interests of the people of Canada to have them secure that road ? I can well understand that it would establish them in their credit, that they would be placed in an entirely different position before the financial world from that which they are in to-day. It would be of immense advantage to them but would it be of advantage to the people of Canada ? If the experiment which the minister is to undertake with respect to the management of the road during the next year be a failure, if it bring about no better results than he is now obtaining, I would like to know whether there is an idea that we should discontinue our operations of that road in favour of the Canadian Northern? If that were the proposal before this House I would unquestionably take my stand against it. I would be recreant to what I deem to be my duty to my constituents, I would be falsifying the record of a life time, if I were to support any such idea. I cannot agree with the Minister of Railways that the Intercolonial Railway must of necessity be the outlet for a transcontinental railway in order to achieve the success which he would like to see it achieve. It must be borne in mind that the Intercolonial was not built for the wheat traffic. It must be borne in mind that in 1903, when we had under consideration the bringing of the produce of the west to the Atlantic seaboard, it was the opinion of the people of this country, it was the opinion of the members of this House, that the Intercolonial Railway should not be that channel of communication, and that by reason of its conditions by reason of its grades, it would be impossible for it to carry that traffic, and if it is true as the minister states, that the Intercolonial Railway must be an outlet for a transcontinental line, why did we not make it an outlet in 1903?
Hear, hear.

My hon. friends think they get some comfort from that idea. I hold and every man on the other side must recognize, that the Intercolonial was not designed for the purpose of carrying the wheat from the west, it was extended to Montreal, to secure the traffic of central Canada, uniting Ontario and Quebec and the maritime provinces. It was intended to unite the provinces of Ontario and Quebec to the maritime provinces. It was never built as a transcontinental line and it was never expected that it would become such a line. If the Intercolonial is given the advantage of management and the advantage of the traffic of the provinces of Ontario and Quebec, if its facilities are enlarged, if its branch lines are extended into the remote sections of the maritime provinces, it will accomplish the object

which led to its construction-not the carrying of traffic from the wheat fields of the west, but the traffic from industrial centres of Ontario. These industrial centres are pouring out each year an increasing quantity of products for which they are seeking a market, and in order to secure that market they require the best possible transportation facilities. They require to reach the remote sections of the maritime provinces at the lowest cost and with the greatest advantage. But under the conditions prevailing with respect to ing Intercolonial Railway and its connecting lines, these advantages are not given the manufacturers of Ontario, and these manufacturers consequently cannot reach those remote markets. The Intercolonial Railway will be a great success if it could but assemble that traffic and distribute it within the zone of its influence. That zone can be widened and extended by the acquisition of these branch lines. And if it is extended and if rates fair and reasonable to the consumer as well as to the manufacturer are afforded, I venture the assertion that the Intercolonial Railway would be an immense success, not merely in bringing together the people of the different provinces, but in earning a surplus which would increase each year. I remember on one occasion I had a computation made as to what the financial returns of the Intercolonial Railway would have been had we charged on our traffic for one year the rates charged on the Canadian Pacific Railway in eastern Canada, and I found that we would have had a surplus on that year's operations o: two and a ha'.f million dollars. Surely with these opportunities within our reach, it is the duty of this government and parliament to place the Intercolonial Railway in such a position that these results will be brought about. My hon. friend the Minister of Railways realizes that. His own argument demonstrated that it could be done, and I am sure that there is no man who would dispute the conclusion, that if it can be done it should be done.
I do not wish to say anything further with respect to any management or any proposed management or method of management. Opportunities for criticism will naturally be offered, but it seems to me that the minister should take into consideration the additional expense involved. I am not one of those who had very great faith with respect to the Civil Service Commission. I venture to declare myself from my place in this House on that subject. We find to-day that we have established a commission at Ottawa for the purpose of doing-what? For the purpose of selecting employees for the civil service in Ottawa, and $30,000 were voted the other day simply to run that commission. But formerly the work entrusted to that commission was
done, and well done, by the heads of the departments. But if this board in connection with the Intercolonial Railway is created, there must of necessity be additional expenses; and while I am not in accord with the Minister of Railways regarding this proposition, because I do not think it is in the interests of the Intercolonial Railway or the proper administration of his department, yet I think that he should be given full latitude to manage that railway in the way he considers the most efficient. I am criticising his proposition, as others no doubt will, but yet it is not a matter of vital concern. The question which is vital, boiled down, is this, that the Intercolonial Railway shall be continued as a government-operated railway, that it shall be extended, that its influence shall be made wider, and that it shall be made better able to do, not the transcontinental business, not the assembling of traffic from the fields of the west, but the gathering up of the products of Ontario and Quebec and distributing them to the markets of the east and to the point of departure to markets beyond the sea. If we should aim to do that, in my judgment we will be fulfilling the expectations of those who have the interests of this country at heart, and assist in developing our industries.

speakeroldname: Mr. W. S. LOGGIE (Northumberland, New Brunswick).
speechtext:
I cannot let this opportunity pass without saying a few words on the very important question before the House. The matter of the construction and operation of the Intercolonial carries us back to the days of confederation when that road was made a link in the chain which binds the maritime provinces to the rest of Canada. As my hon. friend from Westmoreland (Mr. Emmerson) pointed out a few days ago, there is a clause in the British North America Act providing that the construction of the Intercolonial Railway shall commence within six months of the passing of the Act, and we have during the last forty years operated that road as a government railway. In 1896, when the present government came into power, the earning power of that railway was in round numbers about $3,000,000. During the last twelve years by adding the mileage between Ste. Rosalie and the Chaudiere, namely, 112 miles, and between Fredericton and Loggie-ville, 125 miles, we have increased the earning power of that road by $6,000,000. We have increased its earning power 300 per cent, whereas we have not, except by a very small percentage, increased its mileage.
We have therefore to take this position that we can do the transportation from the east to the west and from the west to the east-I do not mean as a portion of a great through line from the prairie provinces; but in the great industrial centres of

Canada, mainly in the commercial metropolis of the Dominion, the city of Montreal, we can gather up a very large proportion of our traffic; and we are handed a portion by the Grand Trunk Railway, according to an arrangement between the government and the company. But I want you, Mr. Speaker, not to forget when we are talking about traffic from the west, which we are not in a position to gather up as perhaps we would be if the railway extended to the prairie provinces, that at the present moment we have a practical monopoly of gathering up the traffic in the east. We are told by the department in reply to the hon. member for Guys-borough (Mr. Sinclair) that the Intercolonial Railway traffic from the east to the west is fifty-six per cent. As far as that fifty-six per cent of the traffic is concerned, what does it matter how many railways there are carrying the traffic from the west to the east? They will not affect it. We have a traffic arrangement with the Grand Trunk Railway Company by which we take their traffic at Montreal in exchange for our traffic to them. When they take that traffic from us, it is surely reasonable that we should have something that we can offer to other roads, if the Grand Trunk Pacific should say that it wanted all the traffic to Moncton. We must not get the blues over this project. It is a matter that has engaged the attention of this country for the last forty years, and there has been adverse criticism by both parties. When the Conservative party was in power, there was adverse criticism by the opposition. I am very glad, however, on this occasion to hear my hon. friend the ex-Minister of Railways (Hon. John Haggart) say: Do not part with the Intercolonial Railway; the time will come when it will be a heritage to the maritime provinces. Let me say, Mr. Speaker, that these are my sentiments -to stand by the tie that binds the provinces by the sea with the provinces of central Canada. The very word Intercolonial means an interchange of traffic. You have this steel road taking Ontario flour from the west to the east, and fifty-six per cent of the traffic of the Intercolonial is from the east to the west; and if it be true that our rates are lower than those of any ordinary railroad, will any gentleman tell me that the people in ;he west are not receiving a share of the benefits arising from those low rates ? It does seem to me that if there are low rates on the Intercolonial Railway, the advantage is mutual. There was 44 per cent of the traffic going east carried over the road during the past year. I venture to say that a very large proportion of that arises in the city of Montreal and is not handed over by the Grand Trunk Railway at all. If we look on the bright side of this matter, we shall be able to realize the picture of Mr. LOGGIE.
the ex-Minister of Railways on the Conservative side of the House (Mr. Haggart) who said to-night that we must not part with the Intercolonial Railway, and I echo in the strongest terms that sentiment. I realize that it is the heritage of the maritime provinces and the link uniting those provinces to the other portions of the Dominion. If you leased the railway for ninety-nine years, you would to all intents and purposes be selling it, and the effect might be to break that tie. I shall not forget very quickly what the hon. Minister of Railways said to-day about linking the Intercolonial Railway to one of the great transcontinental lines. In the Act relating to the construction of the Grand Trunk Pacific, there is a clause providing that the Intercolonial Railway should be linked to the Grand Trunk Pacific from Moncton to Halifax and from Moncton to St. John. That clause reads like this:
Securing to the company running powers and haulage rights over the Intercolonial Railway or any portion thereof, upon such terms as may be agreed upon between the government and the company.
I am sure that is good doctrine. That is using the rails of the people's railway from Moncton to the sea-board, and it does seem to me that it would not be unreasonable to apply the same principle to another great transcontinental railway that will very soon reach the city of Quebec. That is, use the rails of the Intercolonial railway from Quebec to Moncton-retain the management of the people's railway and give haulage rights over it. I	know
that	there	is	objection to	that.	Iknow	that	it	will be said	that	it isa long haul, and that local traffic would not be gathered up. I quite admit that'. It seems to me all the same that some favourable arrangement might be made along these	lines.	I	have another	alternative.
This is a project of mine, and you will pardon me, Mr. Speaker, if I make it known. The Act relating to the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway gives the government this power:
Reserving power to the government to grant running powers and haulage rights sufficient to enable any railway company desiring to use the said eastern division, or any part thereof, to do so upon such terms as may be agreed upon between the companies, or, in the case of their failure to agree, then upon such terms as may be deemed reasonable and just by the government, having regard to the rights and obligations of the lessees.
Now my proposition is this: We will have one of the best pieces of railroad in the world between Quebec and Grand Falls. We have power to allow the Canadian Northern to run over the rails down as far as Grand Falls. Then the country requires in the very worst way a railroad constructed

between Grand Falls and St. John down the St. John valley. Therefore, we have a through road for the Canadian Northern from the Pacific to the Atlantic by using a certain number of miles of the Transcontinental Railway, namely the distance between Quebec city and Grand Falls, and there you will have a road filling a gap which very much needs to be filled, because every hon. gentleman in this House knows that the necessity of a road down the St. John River valley is one of the most urgent needs in New Brunswick to-day. When this gap is filled, a line will be afforded from one ocean to the other ocean. So far as I am personally concerned, that project would satisfy me very well. I would never think of saying to the Canadian Northern, you take over the management of what we have managed for forty years, and administer it. The government have done so that its earnings have increased from $3,000,000 twelve years ago to $9,000,000 this year. Now, Mr. Speaker, so far as the management of the railway is concerned, 1 am willing to listen to any suggestion that hon. members may have to make. They can eliminate the partisan feature from it. 1 he road intersects my county from one end to the other, and I can tell hon. gentlemen that I do not know anything wrong in the management of the road. I do not know that the partisan feature which is dwelt upon so much, affects the revenue in the least, I do not know that there is a man on that railway who is not earning the dollar a day that he receives. So far as I know the railway is well managed, and it is a pleasure for me to compliment the Minister of Railways on the statement he has given us to-day, both as to its management during the year past and also so far as the present year has gone. Now I cannot help but say this, Mr. Speaker, that the great corporations base their expenditures on their revenues and have to pay interest on capital. Their management endeavour to manipulate profits so that the interest for dividends is provided for. If, however, there comes a bad year and earnings do not reach nearly -what was anticipated, the inevitable must happen, namely, no dividend is declared, but as a rule, there is no noise about it. Now, what is the case with the Intercolonial in this regard; it is this: The expenditure and revenue are based on practically an equili-brum, and when a panic year happens, and earnings fall off, then the only result can be>
a deficit, because provision was not made for any great surplus over expenditure. So far as I am concerned I would favour, if necessary, raising the rates 5 per cent all round, 10 per cent if necessary, 15 per cent if necessary. I am satisfied that as a party', and as a people we owe it to ourselves to make that railway self sustaining, knowing that it is the chain
that was forged many year^ ago to bind the maritime provinces to upper Canada, and that chain is clearly provided for in the British North America Act. Therefore I say that for my part I am opposed to the Intercolonial passing into the hands of any corporation to manage it, but I would allow another corporation to use the rails on terms that are reasonable and fair. I am willing to give the Transcontinental most favourable terms from the starting point to the seaboard, I would give them less rates than they could possibly afford, to pay interest on the capital invested, if it used its own rails. Now, Mr. Speaker, any proposition to part with the management of the Intercolonial seems to me like breaking faith with the maritime provinces. I see no reason for pessimism. The prospects are bright. My hon. friend from South Lanark (Mr. Haggart) said that the road could be made self supporting. I do not think there is much danger if the Grand trunk Railway should say they are going to hand over to the Grand Trunk Pacific what was our share of the freight going east. They cannot give it for Campbellton, they cannot give it for Newcastle, they cannot give it for other points between Levis and Moncton, it is true they can give it for Moncton. Let me tell you that they receive more from us than they give us and in a fair exchange we can take care of ourselves.

I do not think this discussion should close without the House hearing from one of the private members from the province of On-ario. We have heard from the Minister of Railways to-night, a statement on the Intercolonial and I must admit that after listening carefully to the statements he madet I came to the conclusion that perhaps after all the opinion I have had in the past was wrong. He made out such a case for the good management of that property that once or twice I began to think that perhaps the Intercolonial was managed better than any other road. I have consulted the report of the Minister of Railways, and studied the figures which are given as regard capital expenditure, and revenue, operating and working expenses. According to my calculations I find that during the 41 years the road has been in opera-tian, the Intercolonial has produced a surplus in 18 years, and in 23 years it has produced a deficit. Then I analysed it a little bit closer. I wondered whether the bad management was all since the present government came into power. I took the number of years in which there were surpluses from 1878 to 1895, and I found that they numbered six and that the number of years in which there were deficits was twelve. The percentage of surplus years was not as great as we would like them to

have been. From 1896 to 1908 I found that the good or bad management, as shown by surpluses and deficits, was a little to the advantage of the present government, as the number of years in which they had surpluses was seven and the number of years in which they had deficits was six.
However, I have got back to the point 1 started from. I have had my own opinion as to the management of the Intercolonial Railway, I have discussed that question with members of this House, I have discussed it with business men outside of the House, in the maritime provinces, in the province of Quebec and in the province of Ontario and in these private discussions every man with whom I have talked has been of the opinion that the Intercolonial can snever be properly and successfully* managed under a government department as it is at the present time. If we feel that, if we believe it, I cannot see why we should not have the courage to stand up and say so. My hon. friend from Westmoreland (Mr. Emmerson) stated that he had cold comfort in the speeches which he had listened to, and I am very much afraid that he will find less comfort perhaps in my few remarks than he had from the others. We are discussing at the present time the theory of government ownership. We have had an opportunity of experimenting with government ownership in this country for forty-two years and over. If we were running a business and we found that one department of it was being carried on at a loss, what would happen? We would change our methods of management or get rid of that particular department of the business. Are we running a business when we are representing the people in this House? Is not this simply a great big business undertaking and should it not be run on strictly business lines? I was very much struck with the statement which was made by my hon. friend the Minister of Railways and Canals and also with another statement which was made by my hon. friend the hon. leader of the opposition. The hon. Minister of Railways and Canals made the statement in his remarks that the views of the political parties on the Intercolonial Railway depend on whether they are in or out. The hon. leader of the opposition made the statement that the Intercolonial has been too much hooked up to political influences. You have these two statements made by prominent members on both sides of this House, and I think that ninety-nine, perhaps one-hundred per cent, of the members of this House believe that these statements disclose the cause of the whole trouble, and account for our failure to properly manage the Intercolonial. If that is the case I think we should face the situation and endeavour to seek a solu-Mr. HARRIS.
tion which will be in the interest of the country at large, because any solution which can be arrived at with regard to the management of this property will necessarily and decidedly be to the interest of the country at large. The first principle of government ownership is to give the people the special utility to be owned and managed by the government at cost. When I say cost I do not figure as my hon. friend from Northumberland, New Brunswick, (Mr. Loggie) does. He says that the revenue and expenditure of the Intercolonial Railway are on an equilibrium. That is very good. If we ran our own private business with the revenue and expenditure on the same kind of equilibrium we would all be in the poorhouse in short order. I am of the opinion that the Intercolonial should be managed in such a manner that it will not only pay its operating or running expenses, but that it will earn a fair and and decent amount of interest on the capital employed in the construction of the property. That is a principle that every hon. gentleman^ I am sure, will agree with. The ouly management I will be satisfied with and I believe the only management that other members of this House will be satisfied with is the one that will produce results of that kind. I was very much surprised to hear the hon. member for Westmoreland make the statement on the floor of this House that local rates in the maritime provinces are lower than they are in any other part of the country. Is that not right?
They are lower than any where in the world.

In that case then the other provinces are having a very decided and great wrong done to them because the people in the maritime provinces have no right to have local rates lower than we have in Ontario or than the people in Manitoba and the western provinces have.

You get your canals
free of tolls.

I do not propose to take up this canal question because I think it is a very dangerous thing to get into any sectional discussion. The hon. membeT for Westmoreland (Mr. Emmerson) tells us that the deficits on the Welland canal are so and so. The only thing I will say about that is that if we have deficits on the Welland canal we have a perfect right to have them for the simple reason that the good old province of Ontario which stands as a buffer state between the east and the west has to pay the deficits; so, why should we not have them if we want them ? Now, we evidently cannot agree as to the best means of managing this property. The hon. member for South Lanark (Mr. Haggart) is

not apparently willing to agree that any of the methods which have been mentioned here to-night would be satisfactory. Others have agreed that a commission would be satisfactory. I personally do not believe that a commission would assist us very much. I do not think that we would get any better results by management under a commission than we get at the present time for the simple reason that I do not believe that we could get a commission which could be completely separated from political influences, and therefore management by commission would have the same drawbacks that we have at the present time.
I am not going to make any suggestion as to how the property should be managed but I am glad the question has come up and that we have had an opportunity of expressing our views and opinions upon it.
I hope, before anything definite is done, that we will have a further opportunity of seriously considering the question with the view of getting together in a fair, proper and reasonable discussion and endeavour to arrive at a solution which will help us out of a position which is not a good one for the country generally and especially for that portion of the country through which the road Tuns.

I do not rise to find fault with this vote, which I may say is a veTy necessary one. I would like, however, to call the attention of the minister to the very unsanitary condition of the present Truro station, and I shall not delay the House more than a minute or two because I feel sure it will be unnecessary to dwell on the matter at any great length. I have in my hand a clipping from a Truro paper which contains a statement signed by Dr. S. L. Walker, health officer of the town of Truro. It is stated in this newspaper that the report of the medical officer is to be forwarded to the Minister of Railways and myself but my copy has not reached me.
Nor mine.

I will direct the attention of the minister to what Dr. Walker says in conclusion, and then I shall send him over the report so that he may read it. Dr. Walker says:
Taken as a whole the Truro railway station is a positive menace to the health of all who enter it for any purpose, and were it under the town's jurisdiction it could be condemned by the board of health.
I would like the minister to look into this matter and have a remedy applied with as little delay as possible.

I certainly agree with my hon. friend (Mr. Stanfield) that there appears to be a very undesirable condition of affairs at Truro station. The report to which my hon. friend refers was brought to my attention by himself but I have not yet received my copy. I can assure the hon. gentleman that I will give it attention. Of course we will get rid of all these things when we build the new station but in the meantime we will look into that report.
